summary: The note examines a series of US telecommunications outages in 2023 and argues that policy change, infrastructure investment, workforce training, new technology and community involvement are needed for a more reliable network. It covers causes such as storms, software updates, aging cables and staff shortages, and quotes affected residents, businesses, experts, lawmakers and regulators. It concludes that collaboration among stakeholders is crucial.
one_line: A roundup of 2023 US telecom outages, their causes, and proposed policy, technology, workforce and community solutions for greater network resilience.
key_facts: On September 3, 2023, widespread internet outages hit Atlanta after a severe storm, leaving residents without essential services for hours.
On October 15, a major telecom provider suffered a network issue caused by a software update gone awry.
A major service interruption in New York City, reported November 12, was traced to failed decade-old cable systems.
Katherine Lopez, head of a national telecommunications workers' union, said on December 1, 2023 that the shortage of skilled workers reduces the ability to maintain, repair and upgrade systems.

Senator Elizabeth Hartley introduced the Telecommunications Resilience Act on October 28 to require providers to have plans to prevent and respond to outages and to promote resilient infrastructure and a skilled workforce.
On September 30, a leading service provider introduced an AI-powered monitoring system intended to predict and prevent outages.
On November 29, Nashville mayor Andrew Benson announced the Community Communications Corps program, in which local residents help identify vulnerable telecom areas during disasters.
On December 15, FCC chairperson Rachel Suarez outlined a regulatory reform vision balancing stringent service quality measures with incentives for innovation, saying reliability is 'non-negotiable'.
Jameson Clark, an Atlanta business owner, reported significant revenue loss because he could not process transactions during the outages.
Lauren Greenfield, an Atlanta mother of two, said her children couldn't attend online classes and she couldn't log into work systems during the outage.
Martin Gonzalez, leader of the Consumer Telecom Equality group, said on October 5 that providers must be held accountable for reliability and security, not just deals.
Decentralized networks are proposed to reduce single-point-of-failure risk by spreading load across more nodes.
A closing panel on December 20 at the Telecommunication Summit in Chicago stressed unity, with Mariah Conway concluding that infrastructure robustness should reflect how interconnected society is.
